   109	
   110	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
   111	of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
   112	the radix point) has type
   113	\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeral}\llbracket{}n,m,10,v\rrbracket} where $v$ is
   114	the value of the numeral, with the radix point deleted,
   115	interpreted in radix ten.
   116	
   117	A numeral containing only digits (let $n$ be the total number
   118	of digits) and a radix point (let $m$ be the number of digits after
   119	the radix point), then an underscore, then a radix indicator (let $r$
   120	be the radix) has the following type:
   121	\begin{Fortress}
   122	\EXP{\TYP{RadixPointNumeralWithExplicitRadix}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
   123	\end{Fortress}
   124	where $v$ is the value of the $n$-digit numeral, with the radix point
   125	deleted, interpreted in radix $r$.
   126	
   127	Every numeral also has type
   128	\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
   129	for appropriate values of \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}.
   130	
   131	
   132	Numerals are not directly converted to any of the number types
   133	because, as in common mathematical usage,
   134	we expect them to be polymorphic.
   135	For example, consider the numeral \EXP{3.1415926535897932384};
   136	converting it immediately to a floating-point number
   137	may lose precision.
   138	If that numeral is used in an expression
   139	involving floating-point intervals,
   140	it would be better to convert it directly to an interval.
   141	Therefore, numerals have their own types as described above.
   142	This approach allows library designers to decide how numerals should
   143	interact with other types of objects by defining coercion operations
   144	(see \secref{coercion} for an explanation of coercion
   145	in Fortress).
   146	\Library\ define coercions
   147	from numerals to integers (for simple numerals)
   148	and rational numbers (for compound numerals).
   149	In \library, every numeral without a radix point has the type
   150	\TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the number types
   151	(\secref{basic-rationals}); each of the five integer types
   152	(\secref{basic-integers}), \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a
   153	coercion from it.
   154	\revision{revival-numeral-type}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
   155	the numeral types above, which no library declares, and did not name the type
   156	that \library\ give a numeral.
   157	The revival decided on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own,
   158	\TYP{IntLiteral}, from which each number type converts, the type the compiled
   159	path's own library gives it, and \library\ now declare it so.
   160	The compiled type checker gives every numeral without a radix point that type.
   161	The interpreter does not yet: it gives such a numeral the type
   162	\EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its value
   163	does not fit in the narrower type, and it is to give it the type
   164	\TYP{IntLiteral} once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
   165	checker.}
   166	
   167	
   168	\marginnote{What is an ``integer'' in this context?}
   169	In Fortress, dividing two integers using the $/$ operator produces
   170	a \emph{rational number};\marginnote{Not if the second integer is 0.}
   171	this is true regardless of whether
   172	the integers are of type $\mathbb{Z}$ (or \txt{ZZ}),
   173	$\mathbb{Z}64$ (or \txt{ZZ64}), $\mathbb{N}32$ (or \txt{NN32}), or
   174	whatever.  Addition, subtraction, multiplication, and division of rationals
   175	are always exact; thus values such as \EXP{1/3} are represented exactly in
   176	Fortress.
   177	
   178	\note{We should give an example with a radix specifier.}
   179	Numerals containing a radix point are actually rational
   180	literals; thus \EXP{3.125} has the rational value \EXP{3125/1000}.
   181	The quotient of two integer literals is a static expression
   182	(described in \secref{static-expr}) whose value is rational.
   183	Similarly, a sequence of digits with a radix point followed by the symbol
   184	$\times$ and an integer literal raised to an integer literal,
   185	such as \EXP{6.0221415 \times 10^{23}}
   186	is a static expression whose value is rational.
   187	If such static expressions are mentioned as part of a floating-point
   188	computation, the compiler performs the rational arithmetic exactly and then
   189	converts the result to a floating-point value, thus incurring
   190	at most one floating-point rounding error.
   191	But in general rational computations may also be performed at run time,
   192	not just at compile time.
   193	\note{This specifies too much about the implementation:
   194	I don't think we should mention a compiler at all, except perhaps as informal discussion.
   195	In particular, wouldn't it be correct if this arithmetic were actually deferred and
   196	performed exactly at run time?}
   197	
   198	
   199	A rational number can be thought of as a pair of integers $p$ and $q$
   200	that have been reduced to ``standard form in lowest terms'';
   201	that is, $q > 0$ and there is no nonzero integer $k$
   202	such that $p \over k$ and $q \over k$ are integers
   203	and $\left| {p \over k} \right| + \left| {q \over k} \right|
   204		< \left| p \right| + \left| q \right|$.
   205	The type $\mathbb{Q}$ includes all such rational numbers.
   206	Relaxing the requirement $q>0$ to $q \geq 0$ adds three more values, which
   207	$\mathbb{Q}$ also includes: \EXP{1/0} and \EXP{-1/0}, the infinite rationals,
   208	and \EXP{0/0}, the indefinite rational.
   209	\marginnote{Is there any subtyping or coercion relationship between \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
   210	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}?
   211	If \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is a subtype of \EXP{\mathbb{Q}*}
   212	then static checking would normally disallow the assignment,
   213	so is this a relaxation to that rule?  If so, the static checker needs to know about it.}
   214	The advantage of these values is that $\mathbb{Q}$ is closed under the rational
   215	operations $+$, $-$, $\times$, and $/$.
   216	In ASCII, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} is written as \txt{QQ}.
   217	See \secref{basic-rationals} for its operations.
   218	\revision{revival-literals}{The Working Draft of February 2011 described
   219	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}} as three types,
   220	said that a value of type \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} assigned to a variable of type
   221	\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} throws a \TYP{DivisionByZero} at run time if it is \EXP{1/0}
   222	or \EXP{-1/0}, gave the ASCII names \txt{QQ\_star} and \txt{QQ\_splat}, and
   223	pointed to \secref{advanced-rationals} for the definitions.
   224	The three are one type now, as in \library\ (\secref{basic-rationals}), so no
   225	such assignment converts or throws; that is also the answer to the margin
   226	note's question whether \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} are related by
   227	subtyping or by coercion.}
   228	
   229	
   230	
   231	\subsection{Pi}
   232	\seclabel{pi}
   233	
   234	The object named \EXP{\pi} (or \txt{pi}) may be used to represent the ratio
   235	of the circumference of a circle to its diameter rather than a specific
   236	floating-point value or interval value.
   237	In Fortress, \EXP{\pi} has type
   238	\EXP{\TYP{RationalValueTimesPi}\llbracket\VAR{false},1,1\rrbracket}.
   239	When used in a floating-point computation, it becomes
   240	a floating-point value of the appropriate precision; when used in an interval
   241	computation, it becomes an interval of the appropriate precision.
   242	
   243	\subsection{Infinity and Zero}
   244	
   245	The object named \EXP{\infty} has type \EXP{\TYP{ExtendedIntegerValue}\llbracket\VAR{true},0,\VAR{true}\rrbracket}.
   246	One can negate \EXP{\infty} to get a negative infinity.
   247	
   248	\note{What about spaces?  That is, is ``- 0'' treated the same as ``-0'', for example?}
   249	Negating the literal \EXP{0} produces a special negative-zero object,
   250	which refuses to participate in static arithmetic
   251	(discussed in \secref{static-expr}).  It
   252	has type \TYP{NegativeZero}.  The main thing it is good for is coercion to
   253	a floating-point number (discussed in
   254	\chapref{conversions-coercions}).
   255	(Negating any other zero-valued expression simply produces zero.)

\subsection{The type of an integer numeral}
\seclabel{revival-numeral-type}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected sections] \secref{literals}; \secref{coercion}.
\item[Change] \secref{literals} says that \library\ give every numeral without a
radix point the type \TYP{IntLiteral}, which extends \TYP{Number} and none of the
number types, and that each of the five integer types, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} declares a coercion from it.
The box of \secref{coercion} says the same of the coercion into
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, and that the interpreter does not yet give a numeral that
type.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; the revival decided
on 29~September 2026 that a numeral has a type of its own, \TYP{IntLiteral},
from which each number type converts, the compiled path's own library's working
version taken in place of the numeral types of \secref{literals}, which no
library declares, and that \library\ take it before the interpreter does, since
the interpreter can give a numeral that type without changing the declarations
its calls reach only once it runs with the static types of the compiled type
checker.
\Library\ declared their numeral type an object extending \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
its arithmetic withheld by the comment ``Do not enable these until coercion is
implemented; doing so will cause all our arithmetic to occur on IntLiterals.''
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/FortressBuiltin.fss}, lines
495--496 before this change, in the revival's repository).
Coercion is implemented on both paths now, and \library\ declare the type as
the compiled path's own library does
(\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi}, lines
390--431): beside the number types under \TYP{Number}, with the arithmetic that
comment withheld, each integer type declaring a coercion from it.
\EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, which that library does not declare from
a numeral, coerce from it too, since \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} coerces from every integer
type (\secref{basic-rationals}) and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} from integer numerals
(\secref{revival-int-float}).
\item[Effect] The compiled type checker converts an integer numeral to the
integer type, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} or \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} that its context expects,
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}64} among them, which refused a numeral
before.
A numeral beside a value of an integer type is converted to that type where no
declaration of the operator is applicable to the two without coercion, and that
type's own declaration of the operator is then the most specific
(\secref{resolving-coercion}); \library\ state on each integer type the
comparisons \EXP{<}, \EXP{\leq}, \EXP{>} and \EXP{\geq}, \OPR{CMP},
\OPR{MAXNUM}, \OPR{MINNUM} and a power with a numeral exponent, which the types
inherited before from a declaration that a converted numeral leaves tied with
those of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64}, \EXP{\mathbb{Q}} and \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
Equality is stated in pairs instead: each integer type declares an \EXP{=}
whose parameter is of type \TYP{IntLiteral}, and \TYP{IntLiteral} one whose
parameter is of each integer type, and each converts the numeral by its
coercion into the integer type and compares by that type's own \EXP{=}.
Inequality is not converted: the top-level declaration of \EXP{\neq}, whose
parameters are of type \TYP{Any}, is applicable to an integer value and a
numeral without coercion, and the compiled type checker selects it and converts
neither operand.
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} states in its api, for the same reason, the additive and
multiplicative operators its body declares.
\TYP{IntLiteral} declares its own \VAR{zero}, \VAR{one}, \VAR{even},
\VAR{odd}, \VAR{floor}, \VAR{ceiling}, \VAR{truncate}, \OPR{DIVIDES},
\OPR{TIMES} and a power with a numeral exponent, which a numeral reached
before as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, since no member of \TYP{Integral} is
applicable to a numeral of that type, even with coercion
(\secref{applicability-with-coercion}).
A numeral given where any integer type is accepted, as the count of a shift,
is converted to the narrowest of \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} and
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}} that holds its value, as \secref{numeral-default} reads a
numeral whose conversions tie.
The interpreter still gives an integer numeral the type \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32},
\EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} by its value, so a numeral reaches none
of the declarations of \TYP{IntLiteral} there.
Its calls of the comparisons, \OPR{CMP}, \OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM} on an
integer type reach that type's own declarations, which answer as the
declarations inherited before did, except that \OPR{MAXNUM} and \OPR{MINNUM}

Some types may be parameterized by \emph{static parameters};
we call these types \emph{generic types}.
See \chapref{trait-parameters} for a discussion of static parameters.
A static parameter may be instantiated with a type or a value
depending on whether it is a type parameter.
\note{

It isn't complete in any case, because of union/intersection types.}
Two types are identical if and only if they are the same kind and
their names and static arguments (if any) are identical.
Two \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} static arguments
(\secref{natparams}, \secref{static-expr})
are identical if and only if they are written alike
once each operation whose operands are numerals is replaced by its value:
\EXP{2\;3} and \EXP{6} are identical,
and \EXP{s_{0}\;s_{1}} is identical to itself but not to \EXP{s_{1}\;s_{0}}.
Two such arguments are known to differ when they are two different numerals;

\section{Types in the Fortress Standard Libraries}
\seclabel{types-libraries}

\Library\ define simple standard types for literals such as
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket{}b\rrbracket},
\TYP{()} (pronounced ``void''),
\TYP{Character}, \TYP{String}, and
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{b}, \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}
(See \secref{literals} for a discussion of Fortress literals).
Moreover, there are several simple standard numeric types.
These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them.
Values of these types are immutable.

The numeric types share the common supertype \TYP{Number}.
Fortress includes types for

content.content:
\chapter{Objects}
\chaplabel{objects}

\note{Properties are not yet supported. Of value objects, only strict
equivalence is supported: the interpreter and the compiled code compare two
value objects of one type field by field (\secref{equivalence}).}

\emph{Objects} are values that have \objecttypes\ described in
\secref{object-traits}.
Objects contain \emph{methods} (described in \secref{methods}) and
\emph{fields} (described in \secref{fields}).

An object is a \emph{value object}, a \emph{reference object},
or a \emph{function object}:
It is a function object if it has an arrow type,
a reference object if it has an object trait type
that is not declared with the \KWD{value} modifier
(see \secref{value-objects}),
and a value object otherwise
(i.e., if it has a tuple type, the type (),
or an object trait type declared
with the \KWD{value} modifier).

A value object cannot have mutable fields,
and it is completely determined by its type,
environment and its fields:
Value objects with the same type, environment and fields
are indistinguishable.
Thus, an implementation may freely copy value objects.
Most objects with simple standard types,
such as booleans,
numeric literals,
IEEE floating-point numbers,
integers of every precision,
and rational numbers are value objects.
%
In contrast,
reference objects are thought to ``reside in memory'',
and are identified by an \emph{object reference}.
A new object reference is created
whenever a reference object is constructed,
so that reference objects constructed separately are always distinct.
What about reference objects that have no mutable fields?
Reference objects include
strings
and aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets.
\revision{revival-object-kinds}{The Working Draft of February 2011 named
arbitrary-precision numbers among the reference objects and gave strings no
kind.
The revival decided on 6~November 2026 that the values of the
arbitrary-precision integer and rational types are value objects, as \library\
declare them, and on 6 and 7~November 2026 that strings are reference objects:
two strings are strictly equivalent only when they are one object, and their
text equality is their \EXP{=}.}
%
Function objects are immutable and have no fields.  Identity is not
well-defined for function objects, and attempting to check whether two
functions are equivalent returns an approximate result.
\secref{equivalence} describes object equivalence in further detail.

\seclabel{value-objects}

An object declaration with the modifier \KWD{value} declares a value object
that is called in many languages a \emph{primitive} value.
The \objecttype\ declared by a value object implicitly has the modifier
\KWD{value}.



The fields of a \KWD{value} object are immutable;
they cannot be changed directly or it is a static error.
However, Fortress allows value objects to have settable fields
as an abbreviation for constructing a new value object with a different
value for one field.
If a value object has a setter method or a subscripted assignment operator
method (described in \secref{subscripted-assignment}),
then the return type of the method must be the value object trait type
instead of \EXP{()}.  When such a method is invoked, the receiver
must itself be assignable, and the value returned by the method
is assigned to the receiver.


For example, here is a value object \TYP{Complex} number:
%value object Complex(settable real:Double, settable imaginary:Double=0)
%  opr +(self,other:Complex) = Complex(real + other.real, imaginary + other.imaginary)
%end
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{value}\;\;\KWD{object} \TYP{Complex}(\KWD{settable} \VAR{real}\COLONOP\TYP{Double}, \KWD{settable} \VAR{imaginary}\COLONOP\TYP{Double}=0)\)\\
{\tt~~}\pushtabs\=\+\(  \KWD{opr} +(\KWD{self},\VAR{other}\COLONOP\TYP{Complex}) = \TYP{Complex}(\VAR{real} + \VAR{other}.\VAR{real}, \VAR{imaginary} + \VAR{other}.\VAR{imaginary})\)\-\\\poptabs
\(\KWD{end}\)
\end{Fortress}
When a mutable variable \VAR{z}:
%var z : Complex = Complex(0)
\begin{Fortress}
\(\KWD{var} z \mathrel{\mathtt{:}} \TYP{Complex} = \TYP{Complex}(0)\)
\end{Fortress}
updates its \VAR{imaginary} field, the following syntax:
%z.imaginary := v
\begin{Fortress}
\(z.\VAR{imaginary} \ASSIGN v\)
\end{Fortress}
can be used as an abbreviation for:
%z := Complex(z.real, v)
\begin{Fortress}
\(z \ASSIGN \TYP{Complex}(z.\VAR{real}, v)\)
\end{Fortress}
So the setter for the field \VAR{imaginary} in \TYP{Complex} would do the
work of constructing and returning
%Complex(z.real, v)
\EXP{\TYP{Complex}(z.\VAR{real}, v)}, and the assignment:
%z.imaginary := v
\begin{Fortress}
\(z.\VAR{imaginary} \ASSIGN v\)
\end{Fortress}
would be construed to mean:
%z := z.imaginary(v)
\begin{Fortress}
\(z \ASSIGN z.\VAR{imaginary}(v)\)
\end{Fortress}


Note that modifying a settable field directly within the value object is
not allowed.  For example, the following:
%imaginary := 3
\begin{Fortress}
\(\VAR{imaginary} \ASSIGN 3\)
\end{Fortress}
within the \TYP{Complex} object means:
%self.imaginary := 3
\begin{Fortress}
\(\mathord{\KWD{self}}.\VAR{imaginary} \ASSIGN 3\)
\end{Fortress}
and because \EXP{\mathord{\KWD{self}}} is not mutable, the assignment is
disallowed.


\section{Object Equivalence}
\seclabel{equivalence}

The trait \TYP{Any} declares the object equivalence operator
\EXP{\sequiv}.  This operator is automatically defined for all
objects; it is a static error for the programmer to override it.  The
\EXP{\sequiv} operator is used to decide whether its two arguments
refer to ``the same object'' in the strictest sense possible.  If the
arguments have different dynamic types---including the instantiations
of all static parameters---the result is always \VAR{false}.  If both
arguments are value objects with the same type, then the result is
\VAR{true} if and only if corresponding fields of the objects are
themselves equivalent as defined by this operator; in particular, two
binary words are strictly equivalent if and only if they contain the
same bit pattern.  If both arguments are object references, then the
result is \VAR{true} if and only if the two object references refer to
the identical reference object (in implementation terms, occupying the
same memory locations in the heap).  If both arguments are functions,
the result is \VAR{true} only if the functions behave identically for
any choice of type-correct arguments.  Even if two functions behave
identically, the fortress implementation is free to return \VAR{false}
when they are compared for object equivalence.

\section{A Numeral Whose Conversions Tie}
\seclabel{numeral-default}

A numeral has a type of its own, from which \library\ define coercions to the
number types (\secref{literals}).
Where the types to which a numeral can be converted are incomparable under
$\morespecificeq$, as \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and \EXP{\mathbb{N}32} are, each
taking a numeral and neither converting into the other, the numeral is read as
a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32}, or as a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}64} or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}} when its
value does not fit in the narrower type.
This holds in either step: in the choice among declarations that are applicable
to the call only with coercion and that the numeral would otherwise leave tied,
and in the instantiation of a type parameter that only numerals fix.
So of the declarations \EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{N}32)} and
\EXP{g(x\COLON\mathbb{Z}32)}, the call \EXP{g(0)} invokes the second; and a
type parameter that only numerals fix, whose bounds \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} and
\EXP{\mathbb{N}32} satisfy and the numeral's own type does not, is
instantiated at \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} when \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} holds the numerals'
values.

The rule settles only a tie that a numeral makes.
Where an argument that is not a numeral leaves the declarations applicable to a
call only with coercion tied, no declaration is the most specific, and the call
is a static error.

\item a \KWD{nat} or \KWD{int} parameter that neither an argument nor the
expected type fixes;
\item the element type of a reduction that only its generator clauses determine

\section{Static Expressions}
\seclabel{static-expr}

\note{Of the static expressions in a size, the interpreter computes a sum, a
difference, a product and a power exactly, and refuses a power at a negative
exponent; the compiled type checker computes each operation on numerals,
refusing as out of range a power it does not compute, and compares other size
expressions by their written form (\chapref{types}); the compiled path
computes a size when it names a class. The compiled type checker does not
infer a \KWD{bool}, \KWD{dim} or \KWD{unit} static argument.}

\emph{Static expressions} denote \emph{static values}.  Conceptually,
a static expression is not evaluated while a program is running, and
thus its evaluation
cannot complete abruptly.  Given instantiations of all static
parameters (described in \chapref{trait-parameters}) in scope of a
static expression, the value of the static expression can be
determined statically.  Static expressions which use a restricted subset of operations can occur as
\emph{static arguments} which instantiate static parameters and
\KWD{where}-clause constraints (described in \secref{where-clauses}).
We define the set of static
expressions by first defining the types of static expressions, and
distinguishing static values from the closely related literal values.
We then describe the expressions that evaluate to the various kinds of
static values.


\subsection{Types of Static Expressions}

There are three groups of traits that describe literals
and static expressions:
\begin{enumerate}
\item The \emph{literal} traits, which describe boolean,
  character, string, and numerals.  For example, the literal \VAR{true} has
  trait \EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket\VAR{true}\rrbracket} and a
  character literal has trait \TYP{Character}.
See \secref{literals} for a discussion of Fortress literals.

\item The \emph{constant} traits, which describe values denoted by

content.content:
(* SEQV by the rule of objects.tex, section "Object Equivalence", under walk: values of different types are never equivalent, value objects compare field by field, floats by their bits, and reference objects, strings among them, only with themselves. *)
component StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk
export Executable

object Pt(x: ZZ32, y: ZZ32) end
value object VPlain(a: ZZ32, b: ZZ32) end
value object VBox(p: Pt) end

same(a: Any, b: Any): Boolean = a SEQV b

run(): () = do
    i: ZZ32 = 3
    j: ZZ32 = 3
    l: ZZ64 = 3
    r: RR64 = 3.0
    n: NN32 = unsigned(i)
    assert(same(i, j), true, "two ZZ32 3s are equivalent")
    assert(same(i, l), false, "a ZZ32 3 and a ZZ64 3 differ in type")
    assert(same(i, r), false, "a ZZ32 3 and an RR64 3.0 differ in type")
    assert(same(i, n), false, "a ZZ32 3 and an NN32 3 differ in type")

    b1: ZZ = 3
    b2: ZZ = 3
    assert(same(b1, b2), true, "two ZZ 3s built apart are equivalent")

    one: RR64 = 1.5 + 1.5
    zero: RR64 = one - one
    nz: RR64 = -zero
    nan: RR64 = zero / zero
    assert(same(zero, nz), false, "0.0 and -0.0 differ in their bits")
    assert(same(nan, nan), true, "a NaN is equivalent to itself")
    assert(same(r, one), false, "a float numeral bound to RR64 and a computed RR64 of the same bits differ in type")

    t1: (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
    t2: (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
    t3: (ZZ32, RR64) = (1, 2.0)
    assert(same(t1, t2), true, "two (1,2) are equivalent")
    assert(same(t1, t3), false, "(1,2) and (1,2.0) differ in an element's type")

    s1: String = "ab" || "cd"
    s2: String = "abc" || "d"
    assert(s1 = s2, "two flat strings of one text are equal")
    assert(same(s1, s2), false, "two flat strings built apart are not equivalent")
    assert(same(s1, s1), true, "a string is equivalent to itself")
    rope1: String = "abcdefghij" || "klmnopqrstuvwxyzABCDEFGHIJKLMN"
    rope2: String = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyzABCD" || "EFGHIJKLMN"
    assert(rope1 = rope2, "two ropes of one text are equal")
    assert(same(rope1, rope2), false, "two equal ropes are not equivalent")
    assert((s1, 1) = (s2, 1), "pairs compare their strings by =")
    assert((s1, 1, 2) = (s2, 1, 2), "triples compare their strings by =")
    assert((s1, 1, 2, 3) = (s2, 1, 2, 3), false, "a tuple of four has no = of its own and compares by SEQV")

    p = Pt(1, 2)
    q = Pt(1, 2)
    assert(same(p, q), false, "two Pt(1,2) are distinct reference objects")
    assert(same(p, p), true, "a Pt is equivalent to itself")
    assert(same(VPlain(1, 2), VPlain(1, 3)), false, "value objects whose fields differ are not equivalent")
    assert(same(VPlain(1, 2), VPlain(1, 2)), true, "value objects whose fields are equivalent are equivalent")
    assert(same(VBox(p), VBox(p)), true, "value objects holding one reference object are equivalent")
    assert(same(VBox(p), VBox(Pt(1, 2))), false, "value objects holding two reference objects are not equivalent")

    f1 = fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x
    f2 = fn (x: ZZ32): ZZ32 => x
    assert(same(f1, f2), false, "two equal lambdas built apart are not equivalent here")

    h1: QQ = 1/2
    h2: QQ = 2/4
    assert(same(h1, h2), true, "1/2 and 2/4 are one rational value")

    assert(same(Just[\ZZ32\](1), Just[\ZZ32\](2)), false, "Just(1) and Just(2) differ in their field")
    assert(same(Just[\ZZ32\](1), Just[\ZZ32\](1)), true, "two Just(1) are equivalent")
    assert(same(char(66560), char(1024)), false, "two characters of different code points differ")
    println("PASS")
end

end

object RC64(re: RR64, im: RR64) end

numbers(): () = do
  i: ZZ32 = 3
  j: ZZ32 = 3
  l: ZZ64 = 3
  r: RR64 = 3.0
  assert(sEq(i, j), "two ZZ32 3s")
  assert(NOT sEq(i, l), "a ZZ32 3 and a ZZ64 3")
  assert(NOT sEq(i, r), "a ZZ32 3 and an RR64 3.0")
  zero: RR64 = 0.0
  nz: RR64 = -0.0
  nan: RR64 = zero / zero
  assert(NOT sEq(zero, nz), "0.0 and -0.0")
  assert(sEq(nan, nan), "a NaN with itself")
end

tuples(): () = do
  t1: (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
  t2: (ZZ32, ZZ32) = (1, 2)
  a: Any = t1
  b: Any = t2
  assert(sEq(a, b), "two (1,2)")
end

strings(): () = do
  s1: String = "ab" || "cd"
  s2: String = "abc" || "d"
  assert(NOT sEq(s1, s2), "two strings built apart")
  assert(sEq(s1, s1), "a string with itself")
end

objects(): () = do
  p = Pt(1, 2)
  q = Pt(1, 2)
  assert(NOT sEq(p, q), "two Pt(1,2)")
  assert(sEq(p, p), "a Pt with itself")
  assert(NOT sEq(VPlain(1, 2), VPlain(1, 3)), "VPlain(1,2) and VPlain(1,3)")
  assert(sEq(VPlain(1, 2), VPlain(1, 2)), "two VPlain(1,2)")
  assert(sEq(CC64(1.0, 2.0), CC64(1.0, 2.0)), "two CC64(1.0, 2.0)")
  assert(NOT sEq(CC64(1.0, 2.0), CC64(1.0, 3.0)), "CC64(1.0, 2.0) and CC64(1.0, 3.0)")
  assert(NOT sEq(RC64(1.0, 2.0), RC64(1.0, 2.0)), "two RC64(1.0, 2.0)")
end

run(): () = do
  numbers()
  tuples()
  strings()
  objects()
  println("PASS")
end

end

coercion today (\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/LibraryBuiltin/CompilerBuiltin.fsi},
lines 433--435 and 475).
The example of \secref{widening} computes an \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} with an
\EXP{\mathbb{R}64} by the declaration on \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} after a coercion from
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, which is what the library now does.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/compile-ladder/rung-rr32-sibling/decision-record.md}
in the revival's repository.
\item[Effect] A value of \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} is not a value of \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}.
Two \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} values combine by the operators declared on
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, into an \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}; an \EXP{\mathbb{R}32} combined
with an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, a floating-point numeral or a \EXP{\mathbb{Z}32} is
converted to \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}, and the result is an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64}; an
\EXP{\mathbb{R}32} is converted where an \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} is expected.
A conversion from \EXP{\mathbb{R}64} into \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}, which can lose
precision, stays explicit.
\item[Original text] The Working Draft of February 2011 names \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}
in no passage of the number chapters; it says that ``32-bit precision floats are
written \EXP{\mathbb{R}32}''
(\nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/preliminaries/overview.tex}, line 579),
that the numeric types are mutually exclusive
----
and strings are reference objects: \library\ declare every kind of string as an
object without the \KWD{value} modifier, so two strings are strictly equivalent
only when they are one object, and their text equality is their own \EXP{=}.
The Working Draft of February 2011 named no kind for strings, and the
team's implementations compared two flat strings by their text and two ropes
by identity.
The full reasoning is in
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/any-carrier-2026-11-06.md}, section~2.4, and
\nolinkurl{explorations/reviews/string-equivalence-2026-11-06.md} in the

#!/bin/bash
# old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...
#
# Runs the old code, the base's: bin/fortress of the batch's one base build, with FORTRESS_HOME set to the
# base build and FORTRESS_CACHES to a private caches folder. If the folder does not exist yet, it is first
# made as a copy of the base build's default_repository/caches (36 MB, 0.04 s). The paths in those caches
# are the base build's own, so nothing is translated, and no worktree is made.
#
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches compile P.fss    the compiled path: compile ...
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches run P            ... then run
#   old-fortress.sh <base-build> <worktree>/tmp/old-caches P.fss            walk
#
# Every cache a run writes goes to the private folder: every cache directory and the logs are under
# fortress.caches (repository/ProjectProperties.java:283-299), which FORTRESS_CACHES sets, and
# bin/fortress_classpath and bin/run_classpath put FORTRESS_CACHES/bytecode_cache on the class path.
# Under the base build a run reads the build, the library sources and default_repository/configuration, and
# writes nothing that stays: the parser writes its error logs beside each file it parses from source and
# deletes them (compiler/Parser.java:349-367), so a compile of a program that exports Executable creates and
# deletes two empty, gitignored logs beside Library/Executable.fsi. Two runs at once may share those two
# names; that is harmless, because the base's library parses without errors, so both logs stay empty and
# a log removed by the other run reads as empty (Parser.java:373-377). Measured in
# explorations/coordinator/build-cache-exploration.md, section 6.
#
# Keep the private folder and your programs outside the base build (the program's own logs go beside it).
# Refuses (exit 2) a base build that is not built, and a private folder inside the base build.
set -euo pipefail
USAGE='usage: old-fortress.sh <base-build> <private-caches> <fortress arguments>...'
BASE=$(realpath "${1:?$USAGE}")
PRIV_ARG=${2:?$USAGE}
shift 2
[ -x "$BASE/bin/fortress" ] && [ -e "$BASE/ProjectFortress/build/com/sun/fortress/Shell.class" ] \
  && [ -e "$BASE/default_repository/caches/bytecode_cache/fortress.CompilerBuiltin.jar" ] \
  || { echo "old-fortress: $BASE is not a built tree" >&2 ; exit 2 ; }
PRIV=$(realpath -m "$PRIV_ARG")
case "$PRIV/" in "$BASE"/*) echo "old-fortress: $PRIV is inside the base build $BASE" >&2 ; exit 2 ;; esac
if [ ! -d "$PRIV" ]; then
    mkdir -p "$(dirname "$PRIV")"
    PART="$PRIV.part.$$"
    cp -a "$BASE/default_repository/caches" "$PART"
    mv -T "$PART" "$PRIV" 2>/dev/null || rm -rf "$PART"     # another run made it first: use that one
fi
FORTRESS_HOME="$BASE" FORTRESS_CACHES="$PRIV" exec "$BASE/bin/fortress" "$@"

import String.{CatString, SubString, EmptyString}
import System.{getEnvironment, getProperty}
export Executable

isSubString(s: String): Boolean = typecase s of
    SubString => true
    else => false
  end

run():() = do
  long: String = "abcdefghijklmnopqrstuvwxyz" || "ABCDEFGHIJKLMNOPQRSTUVWXYZ"
  assert(|long|, 52, "|long|")
  assert(long.depth, 1, "the concatenation is a rope")
  unset: String = "FORTRESS_NO_SUCH_VARIABLE_OR_PROPERTY"

  pathFlat = getEnvironment("PATH", "?")
  assert(pathFlat =/= "?", true, "PATH is set")
  pathRope: String = CatString("PA", "TH")
  pathWide: String = CatString("xPA", "THx")
  pathSub: String = pathWide[1#4]
  assert(isSubString(pathSub), true, "pathSub is a SubString")
  assert(getEnvironment(pathRope, "?"), pathFlat, "getEnvironment at a rope name")
  assert(getEnvironment(pathSub, "?"), pathFlat, "getEnvironment at a SubString name")
  assert(getEnvironment(unset, long), long.asFlatString, "getEnvironment at a rope default")
  assert(getEnvironment(unset, pathSub), "PATH", "getEnvironment at a SubString default")
  assert(getEnvironment(unset, EmptyString), "", "getEnvironment at an EmptyString default")
  assert(getEnvironment(EmptyString, "?"), "?", "getEnvironment at an EmptyString name")

(** Containment
 *
 * The type %Contains[\T\]% "contains" objects of type %T%, in the sense
 * that we can check whether a %T% is a member of a %Contains[\T\]% using
 * %opr IN% and its ken, or using a %case% expression. *)
trait Contains[\T\]
    (** %opr IN% indicates whether %self% contains %elt%.  **)
    opr IN(elt:T, self): Boolean
    (** The %MATCH% operator is used (as a temporary hack) by case when the
        match clause is a %Contains[\T\]%.  We must choose either %=%, %SEQV%, or
        %IN% as appropriate, depending on the type of the LHS. **)
    opr MATCH(x:Any, self): Boolean =
        typecase x of
            x':T => (x' IN self)
            x':Contains[\T\] => (x' = self)
            else => fail("Type error in MATCH of Contains")
        end
end

(** %x NOTIN g% is simply %NOT (x IN g).% **)
opr NOTIN[\E\](x: E, this: Contains[\E\]): Boolean = NOT (x IN this)

(** %g NI x% is equivalent to %x IN g% **)
opr NI[\E\](this: Contains[\E\], x:E): Boolean = x IN this

(** %g NOTNI x% is equivalent to %x NOTIN g% **)
opr NOTNI[\E\](this: Contains[\E\], x:E): Boolean = x NOTIN this

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The one library and the compiled checker

POSITIONS.md:75
- P-169 **The runtime's own 45 native bindings, the arrays' store, threads with `abort`, the task trace and the numerals, name compiled helpers that walk's loader answers with walk's own operations, P-167's device, in three compiled shapes.** Each keeps P-58's form, a bare `builtinPrimitive("…")` naming a helper of `nativeHelpers/` that the compiled path runs; walk's loader answers the name with walk's glue, so walk keeps its `AtomicArray` store, its `spawn` and its numerals, and for these names P-58's walk half bends, as for P-167's two. The arrays' 7, of `PrimitiveArray`, `PrimImmutableArray` and `PrimImmutableRR64Array`: the compiled half by P-164's device, a store trait in `FortressLibrary` whose bindings name helpers of a new `nativeHelpers/arrayOps` over a compiled class that holds the elements; `PrimitiveArray` and `PrimImmutableArray` leave the native component and hold the store in a field, and walk's native object below the trait holds an `AtomicArray`; `PrimImmutableRR64Array`'s two move onto a compiled `double[]` class that no factory chooses until array decision A (P-84, P-85). The compiled store is an `Object[]`, and the compiled transaction tracks its reads and writes by the array and the index (`TXReadSlot`, `TXWriteSlot`): P-84 stores every number type's array unboxed, so a compiled `atomic` write into any array needs that keying, and an array of objects keeps one box an element, not two. Threads, `abort` and the task trace, 6: helpers in a `nativeHelpers` class over the compiled runtime, as the team's `nativeHelpers/runtime.java` is; `Thread`'s `val`, `wait`, `ready` and `stop` raise until the code generator compiles `spawn` (row 82). The numerals, 32: `IntLiteral`'s 8 conversions and comparisons become Fortress text over its `asZZ` before the names batch; the other 24, `IntLiteral`'s 21 and `FloatLiteral`'s 3, name helpers that compute, not the prelude's raising stubs (row 318), at the names batch after a reading review designs their carrier, and walk's loader answers them by one rule per helper class, not by a table of names, still refusing a misspelt name. A test on both paths holds the two halves together where both run; `IntLiteral`'s 29 keep only walk's load check, since no walk numeral is an `IntLiteral` (P-76). Why: every array, vector, varargs list and `args` of the one library is built on `PrimitiveArray` or `PrimImmutableArray`, and a body left on glue compiles to the library's own `builtinPrimitive`, which fails, so by the code's reading a compiled program would raise at its first array; walk's loader carries no element, `Thread` or literal (F-299), and an `Object` carrier would take walk's array writes out of walk's transactions. Detail: `reviews/natives-device-2026-11-07.md`, sections 3.1 to 3.4; the store's shape: `coordinator/CLIMB-BATCH-28.md`, "The questions for the curator, before the launch", Q2.

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## The goal

POSITIONS.md:12
- P-12 **After the switch-over, walk runs the compiled type checker on its programs, and then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts.** The curator wants the checker usable on the programs that walk runs. Today `fortress typecheck` checks a program only against the compiler's prelude, so it is no check of walk's programs (F-9 holds this fact). Walk is not changed for this before the switch-over. After it, walk runs the checker on its programs and so gains their static types; F-9 and F-290 say what walk and the library lack for that step. Walk then uses the static coercions that the checker inserts, in place of its choice on the run-time value (P-59, walk's choice of coercions until the switch-over).

== explorations/coordinator/POSITIONS.md, ## Decisions on record, ### The standard and the sources

POSITIONS.md:24
- P-26 **The team's later decision wins over its earlier one, in a text or in code, where the team made it the language's rule.** P-7 names the texts, from the Working Draft to the POPL 2019 paper. Code counts as a decision where the team built it alike for all its types, or stated its rule in a commit message, a comment or the checker. Code that its author called a stub, and code that works around a limit of the JVM or of the checker, serve only the implementation. The decision that they depart from stands. "Later" is the date of the team's work on the point at issue. The revival revises `Specification/` to follow a later decision. The one library follows it too, in place of the team's earlier code, such as the interpreter's library. Where two later decisions conflict, the goal decides (P-8). The implementers' later word also outweighs unfinished text. Why: the Working Draft's early text was a wish. The type group, the part of the team that built the type checker and the compiler, then worked to make the language run. So they learned what is feasible. They sought performance, and specialization was a must. Their later decisions include the exclusion rule, specialization and the number types of the compiler's prelude, siblings from 2009 to 2012 (P-43). The revival knows less than they did, so it does not second-guess them.

\seclabel{revival-expected-contexts}

\begin{description}

block's expected type whether or not local declarations precede it, and gains
two contexts: a clause of an \KWD{if} expression without an \KWD{else} clause,
whose expected type is \TYP{()}, and a clause of a \KWD{typecase} expression
that has an expected type, its \KWD{else} clause among them, whose expected
type is that of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
The sentence after the list says that the expected type is used also for a call
written by loose juxtaposition, as \EXP{f\;x}.
A second revision adds a third context to the list: the body of a \KWD{label}
expression that has an expected type, and the \KWD{with} clause expression of
each \KWD{exit} expression whose target is that \KWD{label} expression, whose
expected type is that of the \KWD{label} expression.
A third revision adds a fourth: an argument of a call that the section does not
accept with its arguments typed without an expected type, where the argument is
itself a call with inferred static arguments, whose expected type is
the parameter type at its position of each declaration of the enclosing call in
turn, instantiated, where that declaration has static parameters, by the
arguments not so typed and the expected type of the enclosing call; and a

The item of the list of what the chapter does not yet describe, in

revival's decision of 8~October 2026 that these four contexts give a call the
type that the text already requires of them, a clause of a \KWD{typecase}
expression by the rule for the type of the \KWD{typecase} expression.
The text gives each context its type.

#!/bin/bash

Every value has an \emph{ilk},
which is the most specific \emph{type} to which it belongs,
and every object has an environment (see \secref{environments}).
See \chapref{types} for a description of types.
The ilk of a value, and the environment of an object, 
are determined when the value is `constructed'', 
as described below, 
and does not change thereafter.

An object may be a \emph{value object},
a \emph{reference object},
or a \emph{function}.
The ilk of a function specifies the types of arguments with which it may be invoked, 
and the types of the values it may return and/or throw.
The ilk of a nonfunction object 
specifies a finite set of \emph{fields} and \emph{methods}.
% the names and types of these fields are specified by the ilk of the object.
% The ilk of a nonfunction object also specifies its methods.
A field consists of a name, a type, and either a value or a location:
in value objects, fields have values;
in reference objects, locations.
The name of a field is either an identifier or an index.
Only values of type \TYP{LinearSequence}
(defined in \secref{lib:LinearSequence}) or \TYP{HeapSequence}
(defined in \secref{lib:HeapSequence}) have fields named by indices.
Every field in a value object is \emph{immutable}.
Reference objects may have both \emph{mutable} and \emph{immutable} fields.
No two distinct values share any mutable field.

Values are constructed:
\begin{enumerate}
\item by top-level function declarations (see \secref{function-decls})
and singleton declarations (see \secref{object-decls}),
and
\item by evaluating an object expression (see \secref{object-expr}),
a function expression (see \secref{func-expr}),
a local function declaration (see \secref{local-fn-decls}),
a call to an object constructor
(declared by a constructor declaration; see \chapref{objects}),
a literal (see \secref{literals}),
a \KWD{spawn} expression (see \secref{spawn}),
a tuple expression (see \secref{tuple-expr}),
an aggregate expression (see \secref{aggregate-expr}),
or a comprehension (see \secref{comprehensions}).
\end{enumerate}
In the latter case,
the constructed value is the result of
the normal completion of such an evaluation.

\section{Values}
\seclabel{values}

\note{Comments:
1. Operators are bound in an environment just like functions.
    Methods are not values.  They are bound in a type.

2. I'm distinguishing fields from captured variables, even though
   there is no semantic distinction, except that captured variables
   could be shared (but they might not be, and if they are immutable,
   we can't tell anyway).}

\note{Jan: perform promised fixes to definition and usage of environment.
 In particular, environments permit sharing of mutable fields.}

A \emph{value} is the result of normal completion of the evaluation of an expression.
(See \secref{eval-completion} for a discussion of completion of evaluation.)
A value is an object, a tuple or the void value \EXP{()}.
Every value has an \emph{ilk},
in the following sections describing each kind of type in more detail.
Specifically,
the relations are the smallest ones that satisfy
all the properties given in those sections (and this one).



\section{Types in the Fortress Standard Libraries}
\seclabel{types-libraries}

\Library\ define simple standard types for literals such as
\EXP{\TYP{BooleanLiteral}\llbracket{}b\rrbracket},
\TYP{()} (pronounced ````void''),
\TYP{Character}, \TYP{String}, and
\EXP{\TYP{Numeral}\llbracket{}n,m,r,v\rrbracket}
for appropriate values of \VAR{b}, \VAR{n}, \VAR{m}, \VAR{r}, and \VAR{v}
(See \secref{literals} for a discussion of Fortress literals).
Moreover, there are several simple standard numeric types.
These types are mutually exclusive; no value has more than one of them.
Values of these types are immutable.

The numeric types share the common supertype \TYP{Number}.
Fortress includes types for
arbitrary-precision integers (of type $\mathbb{Z}$),
their unsigned equivalents (of type $\mathbb{N}$),
rational numbers (of type $\mathbb{Q}$),
real numbers (of type $\mathbb{R}$),
complex numbers (of type $\mathbb{C}$),
fixed-size representations for integers including the types
{$\mathbb{Z}$8}, {$\mathbb{Z}$16}, {$\mathbb{Z}$32}, {$\mathbb{Z}$64},

- P-25 **`Specification/` stays the standard, and the Types chapter of the team's 2012 restart is cited beside it.** The restart is a new specification that the team began in 2012 and left unfinished (F-166). Where its Types chapter, `Documentation/Specification/Prose/Language/types.tick`, covers a topic, a worker cites it beside `Specification/` as the designers' later word. On the rules that the revival revises, such as the exclusion rule, the chapter is the designers' latest intent, which the goal is to finish, and `Specification/` is revised to follow it. Three of the chapter's passages bear on the specification; P-97 holds how the revision uses the first two. It names the exclusion rule "instantiation exclusion" and gives it in two parts: which instantiations of a generic exclude each other (`types.tick:355-360`), and, in its note, a rule on trait declarations (`:361-376`). The revised `Specification/` takes that form: the first part in its chapter on types, the second in its chapter on traits. It adds a `covariant` modifier for a trait's static parameters, which neither path implements and which is future work, off the path to microGPT (P-62). Third, it says that `Bottom` cannot be written in a program, as `Specification/basic/types-vals-vars.tex` already says of `BottomType`.
- P-7 **The goal is to finish what the designers intended, measured by one program, microGPT, compiled to JVM bytecode and running fast.** The revival judges what the designers intended by the team's own sources: its Working Draft of February 2011, its texts on types and its code. `Specification/` holds the Working Draft as a living document: the revival revises it and states each change (P-95). The texts on types include the Types chapter of the specification's 2012 restart (P-25). In `Papers/`, they include the OOPSLA 2011 paper, Naden's 2012 write-up and the POPL 2019 paper with its technical report. P-26 says when code counts, and which source wins where two conflict. The revival does not redesign the language. A pure-Java microGPT is the baseline that compiled microGPT is measured against: the optimal result, the one to aim at.

content.content:
end

- `(*)` starts a comment to the end of the line. It cannot hold `*)`: the parser ends the comment there and refuses the program. `(* ... *)` comments nest.
- A compiled test with a `run` key ends `run()` with `println("PASS")`, unless a `run_out` key checks its output (below).
- Under walk, `assert(x, y, msg)` checks that `x` equals `y`. It and `=/=` call a type's own `=` only if the type extends a `FortressLibrary` trait that declares `=`, such as `Equality` (ledger row 807). Otherwise they compare by `SEQV` (`revival-changes.md`, "Traits and objects"). If a type `P` has its own `=`, make `P` extend `Equality[\P\]`, or write `assert(x = y, msg)`. The compiler's library declares the two-value `assert` only for `ZZ32`, `String` and `Character`; its `assert(flag, msg)` takes any `Boolean`.
- Do not name a variable or a parameter after a functional method of the library, such as `big`, `even`, `numerator` or `shift`. The disambiguator, the phase that binds names, refuses it: "Variable even is already declared."
- Under walk, a numeral does not bind to `NN32` or `NN64`, and a numeral with a radix point does not bind to `RR32` (ledger row 454). Write `a: NN32 = unsigned(5)`, not `a: NN32 = 5`.

The compiled path's own library, used until the one library replaces it,
declares no rational type.
The floating-point types' rounding methods are not affected; which of them
keep the floating-point type, and what they return at an infinity or a NaN,
is row~330 of the revival's gap ledger.
\item[Original text] \nolinkurl{Specification-1.0-frozen/basic-lib/numbers.tex},
lines 479--481:
\begin{quote}
For types \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^*} and \EXP{\mathbb{Q}^{\#}},
all of these methods simply return the argument if it is
\EXP{+\infty}, \EXP{-\infty}, or \EXP{0/0}.
\end{quote}
\item[Route C] The same under route~C.
A return to the original sentence would need the six methods and operators to
declare a rational result, against their entries' \EXP{\mathbb{Z}}, or would
leave them returning a value outside the type they declare.
\end{description}

\subsection{Which objects are value objects}
\seclabel{revival-object-kinds}

\begin{description}
\item[Affected section] The opening section of \chapref{objects}, its list of
the kinds of objects.
\item[Change] Its sentence on the value objects named booleans, numeric
literals, IEEE floating-point numbers and integers; it now names integers of
every precision and rational numbers too.
Its sentence on the reference objects named arbitrary-precision numbers and
aggregates such as arrays, lists and sets; it now names strings and the
aggregates.
The passage gains one box.
The rule of strict equivalence (\secref{equivalence}) is unchanged: values of
different types are never strictly equivalent, value objects of one type are
when their fields are, a binary word by its bit pattern, and reference objects
only when they are one object.
\item[Rationale] This change does not follow from route~A; it follows two
decisions of the revival.
By the first, of 6~November 2026, the values of the arbitrary-precision integer
and rational types are value objects: \library\ declare the arbitrary-precision
integer as a value object, and the sentence's own list called integers value
objects and arbitrary-precision numbers reference objects, so the text
disagreed with itself and with the library; the library's declaration is the
deliberate word.
By the second, of 6 and 7~November 2026, strictly equivalent means the rule of
\secref{equivalence} on both implementations, with no special case for any type,
and strings are reference objects: \library\ declare every kind of string as an
or more elements are equal only when they are strictly equivalent, and two such
tuples of equal strings built apart are not equal (row~923 of the revival's
gap ledger).
The answers are gated by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleWalk.fss},
\nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/tests/ValueObjectCC64Walk.fss} and, for the compiled
helper, by \nolinkurl{ProjectFortress/compiler_tests/StrictEquivalenceRuleCompiled.fss}.

== explorations/fortress-gap-ledger.md:7-27

## The row template

A row is one line of eight cells, `| # | claim | status | class | spec citation | reproducer | found by | notes / workaround |`, at most 1,200 characters, in the table of its topic section, in number order. A pipe inside a cell is written `\|`. (POSITIONS, "The gap ledger's form"; the proposal behind it is `explorations/coordinator/process-engineering/gap-ledger-archaeology.md`, section 4.)

- **#**: the row's number, the next free one when it is added; never reused, renumbered or given to another row. 148 is vacant.
- **claim**: at most 300 characters, whose first 150 name the defect or the capability: what fails or what holds, and where.
- **status**: exactly one word of seven, with no second status and nothing in brackets:
  - `POSITIVE-VERIFIED`: it works; it ran and its output is recorded.
  - `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`: the specification settles it and the reproducer confirms it. A row with one half fixed stays `NEGATIVE-VERIFIED`, and its notes say which half is fixed.
  - `NEGATIVE-BOUNDED`: the failure reproduces; the mechanisms tried are named and are not exhaustive.
  - `CONTESTED`: unsettled; the notes say why.
  - `RETIRED`: a source's claim falsified here, kept so that it is not derived again.
  - `FIXED`: closed by a landed commit (`ledger.py close`): the claim's first sentence, the test as reproducer, notes `fixed HASH; full text: history, row N`.
  - `DUPLICATE`: a pointer (`ledger.py duplicate`), notes `duplicate of row M; full text: history, row N`.
- **class**: `kind (area)`; `—` only for `POSITIVE-VERIFIED` and `RETIRED`. The kind is one of `implementation gap`, `library gap vs spec`, `library bug`, `design limit`, `deliberate`, `typesetter`, `packaging`; the area one of `parser`, `walk`, `checker`, `codegen`, `runtime`, `library`, `prelude`, `specification`, `tests`, `tools`.
- **spec citation**: the `.tex` file and the section heading in quotes, as `basic/operators/juxtameaning.tex`, "Juxtaposition"; a line number only against `Specification-1.0-frozen/`; `silent` where the specification does not say.
- **reproducer**: one test (its name, or its path under the test folders; an `XXX` test while it is an expected failure) or one probe path from the repository root, at most 200 characters; `none` when nothing in the tree reproduces it, with the command and its output, or the probe's old path, in the notes.
- **found by**: the stream that found it (`climb batch 8 rung I`, `run-c3`, `apl rung 2`), at most 60 characters; no date and no role.
- **notes / workaround**: at most 700 characters: `siblings: N, M` first if there are any; the mechanism, with file:line and the commit it was true at; the workaround; for a closed row, `fixed HASH`.

A path under `explorations/` that is no longer in the tree is read from history: `git show $(git log -1 --diff-filter=D --format=%h -- PATH)^:PATH`.

79:## How a defect is recorded
80-
81-Record every defect that you measure in one of three ways, and say in your report which:
82-
83-1. Your change repairs it: an assertion in your plain gated test. It needs no `XXX` stage.
84-2. It is deferred, and the specification settles it: a gated `XXX` test that asserts the specification's answer. Write it in the change that measured the defect, even if a later change will repair it. If walk crashes on the program, still write the `XXX` test, unlike under 3: the harness counts the crash as the expected failure. A deferred defect of a program that the checker accepts and that then fails the JVM's verification (`VerifyError`), linkage or a range check at run time is one of these.
85-3. It is deferred, and the specification is silent or a conflict leaves it open (`exploring.md`): a test that asserts today's behaviour, and a row in the gap ledger (`records.md`). If no program can observe the defect, or no gated test can pass while it shows, as when walk crashes on the program, write the ledger row only. Its reproducer, the row's cell that names the test, is `none`, and its notes give the command and its output.
86-
87-If your brief does not let you edit the original tree, say in your report which of the three the defect needs, and write a ledger row for it, whichever it needs. A probe that only measures and reports is an example. The change that next works there writes the test.
88-
89-## The order: the test, its failure, the fix, the pass
90-
91-1. Write the test, with a plain name. Write the essence of the defect as a clean, minimal program, not the shape in which a probe met it.
92-2. See the test fail through the harness (`harness-one.sh` or `junit.sh`, `tests-running.md`) on the base's code. Do this in a run that ends before you first build or compile your edit. Under walk, do it before you edit a library source that the test reads. If your tree already holds the fix, run the test through the harness on the old code, as `worktrees.md`, "Running the old code", says.
93-3. Make the fix. See the test pass in your last run after your last change of code.
94-
95-The test needs no commit of its own. A test that comes with no fix, such as one that guards a behaviour that works today, has no failing run: see it pass through the harness.
